evals.prompt: I'm building a habit tracker app with Compose Multiplatform (shared UI for Android + iOS). Build me the home screen: today's habits with check-off, a streak counter, and a weekly progress view. Go with the playful / toy-like style, I want it to feel like Duolingo-level fun, not another grey minimal list. Put the code in HabitHomeScreen.kt.
evals.expected_output: A design brief (preset + dials, palette, type, shape, motion) then a working Compose Multiplatform screen with chunky pressable check-offs, bouncy feedback, a celebratory streak element, accessibility notes, and no generic AI tells.

evals.prompt: here's my profile screen in SwiftUI (evals/files/ProfileView.swift), it's so boring it hurts. redesign it neo-brutalist, thick borders hard shadows the works. keep it native iOS where it matters. write the new version to ProfileView.swift
evals.expected_output: A rewritten SwiftUI ProfileView in a committed neo-brutalist style (hard offset shadows, thick strokes, flat clashing colour, raw type), keeping NavigationStack/system toggles behaviour, Dynamic Type, 44pt targets, with a short note of what changed and why.

evals.prompt: Can you do a UX audit of our Android checkout screen (evals/files/CheckoutScreen.kt)? Tell me what's wrong based on real UX principles, then give me a warm premium redesign, Airbnb-ish. Save the audit as audit.md and the new screen as CheckoutScreen.kt.
evals.expected_output: An audit.md citing named principles (Nielsen heuristics, Fitts, Hoober thumb zones, WCAG contrast, form design per Wroblewski, error prevention) against specific lines, with severity; plus a redesigned Compose checkout in a warm premium style fixing the issues (labels not placeholders, contrast, target sizes, summary visible, single primary action in thumb zone).

evals.prompt: I'm building a SwiftUI app for a small ferry line between Naples and the islands (Procida, Ischia). There are only a few boats a day and the last one back is the one everyone worries about. Build the home screen: the next departures from the user's saved pier, a live countdown to their boat, and a way to buy a ticket. It must not look like every other transit app. Put it in FerryHomeView.swift.
evals.expected_output: No preset named, so the run inventories the product, deals directions with scripts/deal.py and states the chosen id and seed with a reason, writes an owned-idea sentence that passes a competitor test (e.g. built from the last-ferry constraint), and builds a live countdown tied to real departure times. Real pier and boat names, no placeholder data or invented reviews. lint.py run with no FAIL, a scored critique reported, Dynamic Type, 44pt targets, VoiceOver labels and Reduce Motion handled.

evals.prompt: Compose Multiplatform app for students sharing a flat: one shared grocery budget per week that resets every Monday. Build the main screen: what's left this week, recent spends by flatmate, and adding an expense. Don't make it look like a bank app. shared/ui/FlatBudgetScreen.kt
evals.expected_output: No preset named, so the run inventories the product, deals directions (finance-unsafe ones are fine to exclude only if justified; students sharing groceries is not banking) and states id and seed with a reason, writes an owned-idea sentence that passes a competitor test (e.g. built from the Monday reset or the shared kitty), and builds one live thing tied to the remaining budget. Realistic flatmate names and grocery amounts, every state designed (empty week, over budget). lint.py run with no FAIL, a scored critique reported, sp text, 48dp targets, semantics and reduce-motion handled.

evals.prompt: I'm making an iOS app in SwiftUI for Casa Lucia, a six-room guesthouse in Polignano a Mare in Puglia, on the cliffs above the Adriatic. Build the room detail and booking screen: photos of the room, what's included, the nightly price, availability for the next two weeks, and a way to book. We don't have professional photos yet. Put it in RoomDetailView.swift.
evals.expected_output: No preset named and no photos available, so the run inventories the place, deals directions without --have photography (or states why the product has runtime photos), and never builds the screen around grey placeholder boxes. Room photo slots are designed for the real photos to come: fixed aspect ratio, AsyncImage with loading and failure states, and a drawn or tonal fallback. Any found picture shows Polignano's world (the town, the sea, the cliffs), is openly licensed and credited, and is never presented as the room itself. Real availability and a single primary booking action in the thumb zone, with the price visible. lint.py run with no FAIL, a scored critique, Dynamic Type, VoiceOver labels and Reduce Motion handled.

evals.prompt: my Mac app is a small SwiftUI library for people who collect vintage ferry timetables (evals/files/LibraryView.swift). it works but it looks like an iPhone app dragged into a window: big rounded cards, a bottom tab bar, no menu commands. redesign it so it feels like a proper Mac app with its own identity. pick the style yourself. write the new version to LibraryView.swift
evals.expected_output: A rewritten macOS SwiftUI LibraryView in a committed, dealt direction: sidebar (NavigationSplitView) plus content and optional inspector, a toolbar with the primary action, menu commands with keyboard shortcuts, hover and context-menu states, a declared minimum window size, dense rows at Mac sizes (13 pt body, 22 pt controls), the owned idea carried through, and a report that names macOS as the platform, typechecks against the macOS SDK and lints in macOS mode. It must not keep the iPhone layout, a bottom tab bar or 44 pt targets.

evals.prompt: I'm building a Mac app in SwiftUI for freelance subtitle translators. Build the main window: the video clip being subtitled, the list of subtitle lines with their timecodes, and the line being translated (source text above, translation below) with its reading speed. Translators spend whole afternoons in it. Pick the style yourself. Write the SwiftUI code to SubtitleWindow.swift.
evals.expected_output: A macOS SwiftUI window dealt with --platform macos: the subtitle lines as a dense table with timecodes and reading speed (CPS), the video as the canvas, the line being edited as a document-like editor with the system text stack, keyboard-first navigation (next/previous line, play/pause, commit) in menu commands with shortcuts, a declared minimum window size, Mac density (13 pt UI, 22-28 pt rows), and an owned idea from the translator's world. Not a phone layout, not the dark-gradient 'Linear style'.

evals.prompt: I'm building a SwiftUI app for backpackers on multi-day hikes. Build the trip status screen: water left, phone battery, distance and time to tonight's camp, and minutes until sunset, with a way to log a water refill. Make it look like an old green phosphor terminal, Fallout Pip-Boy style. Put it in TrailStatusView.swift.
evals.expected_output: The named style is dealt inside the retro preset (deal.py --preset retro). A phosphor terminal built as the product's own instrument, not a Fallout costume: no Pip-Boy, Vault-Tec or Vault Boy names or art. Readouts in a terminal or bitmap face at integer sizes, running text in a readable mono at body size, phosphor ink with at least 4.5:1 on the ground and no dim green body text, CRT effects (scanlines, glow, cursor blink) subtle and off under Reduce Motion, no flashing. A live sunset countdown tied to the time, a refill action with a state change, Dynamic Type, VoiceOver labels on drawn readouts, 44 pt targets.

evals.prompt: My Android app in Jetpack Compose reminds people to water their houseplants. Redo the home screen as 16-bit pixel art, like an old RPG: which plants need water today, how thirsty each one is, and a one-tap way to water them. Put it in PlantHomeScreen.kt.
evals.expected_output: The named style is dealt inside the retro preset (deal.py --preset retro). Pixel art drawn on an integer grid and scaled nearest-neighbour (FilterQuality.None, or drawn rects), a limited palette, a pixel face for display only with a readable text face for names and body, sp text that still scales, 48 dp targets around chunky art, a water action that changes the plant's state with stepped (frame-based) motion that respects reduced motion, semantics on drawn sprites, and an owned idea from plant care rather than a generic RPG skin.

evals.prompt: I'm building a small Mac app in SwiftUI that keeps a log of my film photography: the rolls I've loaded, frames shot on each, which lab developed them, and which scans I still need to check. Give it a retro old-computer look, your pick of which one. Write the main window to RollLogWindow.swift.
evals.expected_output: A macOS window dealt with --platform macos --preset retro, the direction picked by fit (a bitmap desktop, phosphor terminal or pixel sprite Mac form) and named with its Deal line. The real title bar and traffic lights stay real, with no fake title bar drawn on the window; sidebar navigation, a minimum window size, menu commands with shortcuts, Mac density. Retro faces at integer sizes for titles and readouts, a readable face for text, no glow on type, every text tier at 4.5:1, no Apple or Microsoft marks (the rainbow apple, Happy Mac, Chicago, the Windows flag). An owned idea from film photography (a contact sheet, a roll's frame counter, a lab ticket).

evals.prompt: I'm building a Mac app in SwiftUI for home bakers who make sourdough. Build the main window for a bake day: the recipe being made with its steps, every ingredient scaled by weight for the loaves they're making, the timers running for the current step (bulk ferment, proof), and when the starter was last fed. People keep it open on the kitchen counter all day. Pick the style yourself. Write the SwiftUI code to BakeDayWindow.swift.
evals.expected_output: A macOS window dealt with --platform macos (no preset named): the bake's steps with the current one leading, ingredients in grams scaled to the number of loaves (baker's percentages a plus), live timers driven by the clock for the current step, the starter's last feed and its peak window, readable across a kitchen at a glance and dense enough for a Mac. Menu commands with shortcuts for the daily actions (start or pause a timer, next step), a declared minimum window size, not a stretched phone layout, and an owned idea from the baker's world rather than a generic recipe card.

evals.prompt: I'm building a SwiftUI iPhone app for people who manage several daily medications. Many of our users are over 65; some use VoiceOver or Voice Control, many keep their phone on the largest text sizes, and some have a tremor. A regional health system wants to roll it out and needs our Accessibility Conformance Report (VPAT, WCAG 2.2 AA) before they sign. Build the Today screen: the doses due today in time order (medicine, strength, with food or not), marking a dose as taken or skipped, what's overdue, and the refill that's running low. Pick the style yourself. Put it in TodayDosesView.swift.
evals.expected_output: No preset named: the run inventories the product, deals a direction for a health app (calm, not neo-brutalist), and builds a Today screen whose doses are real controls: a Button or Toggle with a style, or a custom control that exposes name, role and taken/skipped state to VoiceOver, with Voice Control names that match the visible words. Overdue is shown by text or a glyph as well as colour. Text uses Dynamic Type to the accessibility sizes and the layout stacks rather than clips at AX5; targets are 44 pt or more with room for a tremor (no swipe-only actions). Status changes are announced. lint.py has no FAIL; the large-text frame is rendered and read; the report states conformance per WCAG 2.2 AA criterion in VPAT terms with reasons, and says what was not tested with assistive technology.

how_to_run: See evals/README.md. Each eval is a full build session: run it with the skill and without it (baseline), grade both with grade.py, then judge screenshots blind with references/critique.md. Ask the user before running: 6 evals x 2 configs = 12 sessions per iteration.
